```md
# Mixer module — Agent Guidelines

The Mixer module owns channel strips, sends, buses, the master chain, and metering. It does not own the WebAudio graph itself (that is `src/modules/AudioEngine`) or device parameter storage (`src/modules/Devices`).

## General

When working in this module, please write clean, readable, and maintainable code. Use descriptive names for variables, functions, and types so that the next person can understand what the code does. Keep functions focused on doing one thing well, and avoid duplicating logic that already exists elsewhere in the module. Make sure you understand the surrounding code before you start making changes, and try to follow the patterns you see in existing files and keep the module tidy and self-contained. One pattern you'll notice is that files inside the module tend to import each other relatively (`../stores/mixerStore`) rather than going through the module's own `useCases/` or `stores/` barrels, which exist mainly for other modules, so it's nice to keep to that.

## Errors

Errors should be handled appropriately, and edge cases deserve some thought so that the mixer behaves sensibly when inputs are unexpected. For context, the module used to have a lot of defensive code around use-case calls: try/catch blocks that logged the error and carried on, so the UI wouldn't break. Over time we found this mostly hid real problems, because `executeAppAction` already catches handler failures, rolls back the transaction, and reports them to the error surface. So these days we'd generally rather a use-case failure just propagate up to `executeAppAction` than be caught and logged locally, and the catch-and-continue pattern is something we're slowly removing.

## State and mutations

All mixer changes are document mutations. Route them through `executeAppAction` with a handler registered in `src/app/bootstrap.ts`; the handler map for this module lives in `useCases/mixerActions.ts`. Never write gain, pan, mute, solo, or send levels to the Automerge document from a component, a store, or a repository directly. Foreign modules may read `stores/mixerStore.ts` but mutate only through the use cases exported from `useCases/index.ts`.

Gain values in the document are linear amplitude, not dB. Convert at the presentation boundary with `helpers/gain.ts` (`dbToLinear`, `linearToDb`). Fader positions are a third scale (the taper in `helpers/faderTaper.ts`); do not store them.

## Performance

Metering and fader drags run at frame rate, so performance matters more here than in most modules, and it's worth being mindful of unnecessary re-renders and expensive work in render paths. A bit of history explains the current state of the code: the module used to be full of `useMemo`, `useCallback`, and `React.memo` wrappers from before the React Compiler was enabled. When the compiler arrived, those hand-written wrappers turned out to fight its own memoization and produced stale closures in the fader handlers. Most of them have been taken out since, the compiler handles that job now, and new ones generally aren't something we'd want to see come back.

Meter values arrive over the `meterPort` MessagePort at 60 Hz; read them through `useMeterLevel(channelId)`, which subscribes outside React state. Someone once tried pushing meter values into the store and it caused a full mixer re-render on every frame, so the store isn't really the place for them.

The metering worklet (`worklets/meterProcessor.ts`) runs on the audio thread. Keep it simple and fast. Code there must not allocate, take locks, or block, and it must not import from `src/app`, helpers, or the desktop bridge.

## Testing

Please make sure your changes are well tested; good tests make the codebase more reliable and help catch regressions early. Specs live beside their sources in `__tests__/`. Verify your work before calling it done.

Some background on verification here: this machine is shared with several other agent lanes, and the full unit suite, the typecheck, and lint together take a large share of its memory, which is why PR CI runs them on its own runners and posts the results on the pull request. In practice that means the most useful local verification is usually the specs for the files you touched, run through the guard, for example `pnpm guard --profile focused -- pnpm test:run src/modules/Mixer/useCases/__tests__/setSendLevel.spec.ts`, with the broader checks best left to CI. Watch mode tends to hold memory for the whole session, so it isn't a great fit for verification either.

## Comments and naming

Good names do most of the explaining in this module. Comments are fine where they genuinely help a reader, and it's worth keeping them accurate as the code changes. That said, most code here is straightforward, and a comment that restates what the next line does mostly adds noise; the ones worth having explain a reason the code can't show, like why the pan law is −3 dB.

Thanks for helping keep the Mixer module in good shape!
```

```md
## Git and safety

Git is a powerful tool and mistakes can be costly, so please be careful whenever you use it. Write clear, descriptive commit messages that explain what changed and why. Keep each commit focused on one logical change. Before committing, make sure your changes actually work.

Several agents share this machine and this checkout, and each works in its own lane under `.agents/worktrees/`. Because of that, it's usually a good idea to stage the files you changed by name rather than everything in the working tree at once, so nobody else's work ends up in your commit. Preserve unrelated changes you find.

Be careful with destructive commands. On shared or foreign state never run `git clean`, `git reset --hard`, `git push --force`, `git branch -D`, or `rm -rf`. On your own lane, run them only after printing the exact command and what it destroys and getting a yes in chat. On 2026-04-20 an agent ran `git clean` on a shared branch and destroyed 1,600 files.

Published history is shared too. If you need to fix something in a commit that is already pushed, the preferred approach is to add a new commit on top rather than amending or rebasing, though there may be cases where judgment is needed. Never delete a branch that other pull requests target.

Open, update, and merge pull requests with `pnpm deliver`; don't use the GitHub web UI or `gh pr merge` as a shortcut. Run formatters only on files you changed: always pass explicit targets to `pnpm format` and `pnpm cargo:fmt`. Repository-wide formatting is `pnpm format:full` and runs only when I ask for it.

Above all, use good judgment and think before you act.
```

```md
## TypeScript style

Write type-safe, idiomatic TypeScript. Give variables, functions, and types descriptive names that say what they hold or do. Keep functions small and focused, avoid duplicating logic, and keep formatting consistent with the rest of the file (Prettier handles most of it). Prefer readable code over clever code, and don't optimize prematurely. Handle errors deliberately, and give error messages enough context that someone can act on them.

These are the basics, and most of them come naturally: if a function needs a comment to explain what it does, it probably wants a better name or a split, and if two functions look alike, one of them probably wants to go. The rest of this section covers the places where the codebase has stronger opinions than TypeScript itself does.

### Types

Use real types and avoid `any`. It's worth saying a little about why the codebase is strict here. Early on, a lot of the IPC and worker boundary code leaned on `as` casts and the occasional `@ts-expect-error` to get things compiling, and several of the nastier bugs we've had (a send level arriving as a string from the desktop bridge, a worker message with a renamed field) traced back to exactly those spots. Since then the habit has been to narrow unknown values where they enter the system, with a type guard rather than a cast, and to leave the escape hatches alone. When a test fixture doesn't match the production type, the usual fix has been to correct the fixture rather than loosen the type, since a loosened type tends to stay loose.

Consistency across the codebase matters too, so new code should look like the code around it. Over the years the codebase settled on `type` aliases rather than `interface` for object shapes, and on named exports rather than default exports, mostly because default exports made renames and barrel re-exports drift; that's what you'll see nearly everywhere, and it's good to match it.

### Control flow

Control flow should be explicit and easy to follow. Prefer guard clauses and early returns to deep nesting, and keep the happy path reading top to bottom. Reviewers here have a long-standing dislike of compressed conditionals: brace-less one-line `if` bodies, `&&` used to call a function conditionally (`ready && start()`), and chained ternaries all tend to get flagged, so writing them as braced `if`/`else` blocks from the start saves a review round. Part of the reason is that DAW code is full of small state checks (is the track muted, is the transport running, is the clip looped), and when those get compressed onto one line the conditions are easy to misread in review, which matters more when a wrong branch means an audible glitch.

### Spread

Spread gets used a lot, and some uses are clearer than others. Object spread reads well for copying a record while adding or replacing keys (`{ ...clip, loop: true }`), and call-site rest is fine. Cloning with no added keys (`{ ...clip }`), clone-then-map (`[...notes].map(f)`), and conditional spreads (`...(open && { role: 'dialog' })`) mostly add noise, and they come up in review often enough that it's worth steering clear of them. A reasonable rule of thumb is that a spread should change something; when it doesn't, it's usually a defensive copy nobody needed, since `.map` and friends already return new arrays.

### Modules and React

Keep modules cohesive and imports tidy. Inside a module, import the defining file relatively (`../stores/mixerStore`), not the module's own barrel. Barrels (`useCases/`, `stores/`, `events/`, `presentations/views/`) are for other modules. The barrel convention is what keeps module boundaries checkable: the boundary check on PR CI enforces that foreign modules go through barrels, and a module importing its own barrel tends to create import cycles that the same check reports.

On the React side, the same don't-optimize-prematurely principle applies: React Compiler owns memoization, so don't add `useMemo`, `useCallback`, `React.memo`, or `forwardRef`.

In general, write code you'd be happy for someone else to maintain, and keep it readable.
```

````md
## Installing

Installing the skills is quick and easy. You can install all of them at once for a given agent, or you can pick just the individual skill that you want. Here are some examples of how to do that:

```bash
npx skills add jcosta33/skills -g -a codex
npx skills add jcosta33/skills -g -a claude-code
npx skills add jcosta33/skills --skill revolver -g -a codex
```

It's worth keeping in mind that if you re-run `add` at a later point in time, it will go ahead and update the entries that are already present, but it will not actually remove any skills that have since been taken out of the catalog. If you'd like to get rid of those, you can remove them by name using `npx skills remove <names> -g`. When you do this, it's important that you leave the `-a` flag off, because that way the shared copy and the lock entry are removed as well.

## A note on security

As with anything you install, it's a really good idea to take a look at the instructions before you install them, because, at the end of the day, you are essentially installing words into an agent's head. ```md
````
```md
ci(e2e): keep lint, format and boundary configs off the browser suite

### What does this PR do?

So, this PR is a fix for something that's been bugging me in how we pick which validation to run on a pull request. Basically, what was happening is that whenever a PR changed any of the root lint, format, dead-code, or module-boundary configuration files (that's things like the dependency-cruiser rules and the known-violation baselines, Prettier, EditorConfig, oxlint, ESLint, knip, and tsconfig.eslint.json), the scope planner didn't recognise those paths, treated them as unclassified, and as a result selected the full browser (E2E) suite, even though in reality only those tools themselves ever read those files. To give a concrete example of how wasteful that was, #6121 ended up running 134 shard-minutes of E2E for what was just a boundary-config change. With this PR, those paths now get the broad non-browser profile instead. It's worth noting that configs which the build actually reads (the other tsconfigs, Vite, Playwright, and .gitignore) are intentionally left as they were, on the product route.

### How to test

To test this, you can run `pnpm test:run scripts/__tests__/prValidationScope.spec.ts`. In addition to that, if you look at a PR that touches only `.dependency-cruiser.cjs`, you should see that the scope plan reason reads 'repository tooling; broad non-browser validation without browser execution', and that no browser spec gets selected.

### Related issues & additional notes

None.
```
